messages.subject: Citations compare secr.fit and openCR.fit
parts:
Hi Murray,

I prefer to use openCR.fit over secr.fit for a lot of my abundance estimates. I have relatively long lived species (13+ years for boodies) that are really trap happy, monitored twice a year, and contained within a fenced enclosure. Despite the lack of GOF testing in openCR I’m convinced it does a better job of estimating abundance because it acknowledges that my populations are open temporally.

That said, journal reviewers with experience in Program MARK are being a real pain in the butt asking for AIC tables to prove that individual covariates should be included (or not). I haven’t used trap covariates (yet) because I work in a fenced enclosure and we know that boodies in particular will travel well outside their normal range for peanut butter.

Can you please suggest some citations for responding to these sorts of comments from reviewers? If I recall correctly, there is a PhD thesis produced during the development of openCR?

Thanks,

Cheryl

messages.subject: Re: Citations compare secr.fit and openCR.fit
parts:
Cheryl
There's no thesis relating to openCR, just the Efford & Schofield Biometrics paper.
I don't quite understand your problem. You can do AIC with openCR, can't you? I tend to think openCR is better kept for questions on survival, recruitment and movement. For density it complicates model selection no end. However, I can imagine scenarios for which within-primary-session data are so sparse that string sessions together is the only way out. Sorry to complicate things by questioning your chosen path. Either way I have a fairly aggressive view towards model selection pedants: at some point you make a biologically informed judgement on what matters and go with that.
Murray
